blocks.text: After a deep forearm laceration, a surgeon repairing the median nerve aligns individual fascicles under a microscope, because the connective tissue wrappings of a nerve guide which axons reconnect with which. The same wrappings, the neurons they carry and the glial cells that insulate them explain how nerves conduct and why they can regrow.

blocks.markdown: Nervous tissue consists of **neurons**, which conduct signals, and **glia**, which support them. A typical multipolar neuron has a **soma** (cell body), **dendrites**, one **axon** and its terminals.

rows: Large pale euchromatic nucleus with prominent nucleolus; basophilic Nissl bodies (clusters of rough ER and ribosomes)
Branching processes with Nissl bodies in proximal parts
Receive synaptic input and carry it toward the soma
Cone-shaped origin of the axon, free of Nissl bodies
Site where action potentials are usually initiated
Long process, no Nissl bodies; may be myelinated
Conducts action potentials away from the soma
blocks.caption: Parts of a neuron

blocks.markdown: By shape, neurons are **multipolar** (many dendrites, e.g. motor neurons), **bipolar** (one dendrite and one axon, e.g. retina) or **pseudounipolar** (a single process dividing into two, e.g. dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons).

rows: Structural and metabolic support, K+ buffering, foot processes on capillaries that help form and maintain the blood-brain barrier; GFAP-positive
Forms myelin; one cell myelinates segments of several axons
Resident macrophages: phagocytose debris and mediate immune defence
Forms myelin; one Schwann cell myelinates one internode of one axon; also ensheaths unmyelinated axons and guides regeneration
blocks.caption: Glial cells compared (ependymal cells line the ventricles and satellite cells surround ganglion neurons)

blocks.title: Which glial cell?
blocks.prompt: In demyelinating disease of the optic nerve, myelin is lost around many axons of the CNS. Which cell normally forms this myelin, and how does it differ from the PNS cell?

steps.text: CNS myelin is formed by oligodendrocytes.
One oligodendrocyte extends processes to myelinate segments of several axons.
In the PNS, each Schwann cell forms a single myelin segment (internode) on one axon, and the gaps between internodes are the nodes of Ranvier.

blocks.answer: Oligodendrocytes; one cell serves several axons, whereas a Schwann cell serves one internode of one axon.

blocks.markdown: **Peripheral nerve connective tissue.** Each axon with its Schwann cell is surrounded by **endoneurium**, delicate loose connective tissue with capillaries. A bundle of axons (a **fascicle**) is enclosed by **perineurium**, concentric layers of flattened cells joined by tight junctions that act as a blood-nerve barrier. The whole nerve is bound by **epineurium**, dense irregular connective tissue with larger vessels and fat. Fascicles of peripheral nerves range from a few hundred micrometres to a few millimetres across.

blocks.caption: Connective tissue layers of a peripheral nerve

blocks.markdown: **Scale from magnification.** True size = size on the image / total magnification. For example, a fascicle measuring 40 mm on an image at 100x is $40/100 = 0.4$ mm, or 400 micrometres.

blocks.title: Sizing a fascicle
blocks.prompt: A cross-section image printed at 50 times magnification shows a fascicle 30 mm across. What is its true diameter?

steps.text: Convert 30 mm on the image into the real size by dividing by magnification: 30 / 50 = 0.6 mm.
0.6 mm is 600 micrometres, in the plausible range for a peripheral nerve fascicle.

items: Neuron: dendrites receive, soma synthesises, axon hillock initiates, axon conducts, terminal releases.
CNS glia: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia; PNS: Schwann cells.
Nerve layers from inside out: endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Do not mix up Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes: they form myelin in the PNS and CNS respectively, and demyelinating diseases of each target different cells. Likewise, do not label the perineurium as the outermost layer; that is the epineurium.

points: Neurons receive in dendrites, integrate in the soma, initiate at the axon hillock, conduct along the axon and release at terminals.
Astrocytes support and help form the blood-brain barrier, oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells make myelin in the CNS and PNS, and microglia act as CNS macrophages.
A nerve has endoneurium around axons, perineurium around fascicles and epineurium around the whole nerve.

questions.stem: In a stained section of a spinal cord anterior horn, large neurons show coarse basophilic clumps in the cytoplasm that extend into dendrites but not into the axon. What are these clumps?

options.text: Nissl bodies, which are rough ER and ribosomes
Neurofibril bundles of myelin
Synaptic vesicles
Lipofuscin granules from the nucleus

questions.correctOptionText: Nissl bodies, which are rough ER and ribosomes

distractorRationale.b: Myelin is formed by glia, not a cytoplasmic neuron structure.
distractorRationale.c: Vesicles are in terminals and not visible as clumps by light microscopy.
distractorRationale.d: Lipofuscin is a pigment, not basophilic clumps.

questions.explanation: Rough ER and ribosomes make protein and are basophilic, appearing as Nissl bodies in the soma and proximal dendrites. They are absent from the axon hillock and axon.

questions.stem: At which part of a motor neuron is an action potential usually initiated?

options.text: The axon hillock and initial segment
The distal dendrite
The axon terminal
The nucleolus

questions.correctOptionText: The axon hillock and initial segment
questions.explanation: Synaptic inputs sum at the axon hillock, where the density of voltage-gated sodium channels makes it the usual site of initiation. Dendrites mostly receive, and terminals release.

questions.stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis has plaques of myelin loss in the brain, whereas another with Guillain-Barre syndrome has demyelination of peripheral nerves. Which pair of myelinating cells is primarily affected?

options.text: Oligodendrocytes in multiple sclerosis and Schwann cells in Guillain-Barre syndrome
Schwann cells in multiple sclerosis and oligodendrocytes in Guillain-Barre syndrome
Astrocytes in both
Microglia in both

questions.correctOptionText: Oligodendrocytes in multiple sclerosis and Schwann cells in Guillain-Barre syndrome
questions.explanation: CNS myelin comes from oligodendrocytes and PNS myelin from Schwann cells, so diseases that attack each have different targets and clinical patterns.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of a brain capillary shows its wall almost entirely covered by the expanded end-feet of cells that stain for glial fibrillary acidic protein. Which cell is this and what is a main role?

options.text: Astrocyte, helping maintain the blood-brain barrier
Oligodendrocyte, forming myelin around the capillary
Microglia, forming the capillary basement membrane
Schwann cell, guiding axon regeneration

questions.correctOptionText: Astrocyte, helping maintain the blood-brain barrier

distractorRationale.d: Schwann cells are in the PNS.

questions.explanation: GFAP marks astrocytes, whose perivascular end-feet help induce and maintain the tight endothelium of the blood-brain barrier. They also buffer extracellular potassium.

questions.stem: In a nerve cross-section, a thin ring of flattened cells joined by tight junctions surrounds each bundle of axons. Which layer is this and what is its function?

options.text: Perineurium, forming a blood-nerve barrier around a fascicle
Endoneurium, surrounding single axons
Epineurium, bounding the whole nerve with dense connective tissue
Myelin sheath of a single axon

questions.correctOptionText: Perineurium, forming a blood-nerve barrier around a fascicle

distractorRationale.b: Endoneurium is loose connective tissue around axons.
distractorRationale.c: Epineurium is dense irregular connective tissue and surrounds the whole nerve.
distractorRationale.d: Myelin is formed by Schwann cells, not a layer of connective tissue.

questions.explanation: The perineurium encloses each fascicle and its tight junctions limit diffusion into the endoneurial space, forming the blood-nerve barrier.

questions.stem: A cross-section of the sciatic nerve is photographed at 20 times magnification and one fascicle measures 24 mm across on the print. Calculate the true fascicle diameter in millimetres.
questions.explanation: True size = image size / magnification = 24 / 20 = 1.2 mm, which is in the plausible range for a large nerve fascicle (hundreds of micrometres to a few millimetres).

questions.stem: An electron micrograph taken at 5000 times magnification shows a myelinated axon whose cross-section measures 30 mm on the print. Calculate the axon diameter in micrometres.
questions.explanation: True size = 30 mm / 5000 = 0.006 mm = 6 micrometres, a typical size for a myelinated peripheral axon.

questions.stem: Compare the roles of astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and Schwann cells.
markingGuide: Astrocytes: CNS support, K+ buffering, blood-brain barrier via end-feet.
Oligodendrocytes: CNS myelin, one cell myelinates several axons.
Microglia: CNS resident macrophages that phagocytose debris.
Schwann cells: PNS myelin, one internode per cell; ensheath unmyelinated axons and support regeneration.
questions.explanation: The key is pairing each glial cell with its location and main function. Myelin-forming cells differ between CNS and PNS.

questions.stem: Describe the endoneurium, perineurium and epineurium of a peripheral nerve and explain how the structure of the perineurium protects the axons.
markingGuide: Endoneurium: loose connective tissue around individual axons with capillaries.
Perineurium: concentric layers of flat cells around a fascicle.
Epineurium: dense irregular connective tissue around the entire nerve with larger vessels and fat.
Perineurial tight junctions form a blood-nerve barrier limiting entry of substances to axons.
Correct order from inside to outside.
questions.explanation: The layers are nested from axon to whole nerve. The perineurium is the barrier layer because its cells are joined by tight junctions.

questions.stem: Name the parts of a multipolar neuron and state the function of each, including why Nissl bodies are absent from the axon.
markingGuide: Soma synthesises protein and contains Nissl bodies (rough ER).
Axon conducts impulses away; terminal releases neurotransmitter.
Nissl bodies are absent from the axon hillock and axon, since protein synthesis is concentrated in the soma.
questions.explanation: A good answer assigns a function to every part and links Nissl bodies to protein synthesis in the soma.

questions.stem: A peripheral axon is crushed and the distal part degenerates; regeneration then occurs along tubes of Schwann cells inside the endoneurium. Which statement best explains why peripheral nerves regenerate better than CNS tracts?

options.text: Schwann cells and the endoneurial tube provide a supportive path for regrowing axons
Oligodendrocytes guide regrowing axons in the periphery
The epineurium regrows axons directly
Microglia replace the axon

questions.correctOptionText: Schwann cells and the endoneurial tube provide a supportive path for regrowing axons

distractorRationale.c: The epineurium is connective tissue and not a source of axons.

questions.explanation: After injury, Schwann cells clear debris, proliferate and form guiding columns within the endoneurial sheath, which allows axons to regrow. Such a supportive environment is less available in the CNS.
